query: Consider the following context: Constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations are important in developing alloys. In that context, which method can be used for control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Isothermal aging can be used to control phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys by tuning the chemical ordering and morphology of precipitated phases, thereby modulating the alloy’s mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy containing FCC and B2 phases.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the alloy to isothermal aging at different temperatures (e.g., 600°C vs. 750°C) for a fixed time followed by rapid quenching.
generation.conditions: Aging temperatures around 600°C and 750°C for 20 hours with controlled heating and quenching rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Temperature-dependent formation and evolution of Ni3Al-like L1₂ ordered domains along with changes in phase boundary morphology (such as the presence of jagged, high-energy phase boundaries or Cr-rich particle free zones).
generation.mechanism: At lower aging temperatures (600°C), enhanced chemical ordering leads to the formation of perfectly ordered, small L1₂ domains with high interfacial energy and jagged phase boundaries, which promote planar slip and strain localization (embrittlement). At higher aging temperatures (750°C), a shift toward off-stoichiometric, weakly ordered domains and smoother phase boundaries (with dissolved Cr-rich particles) facilitates cross-slip and more uniform deformation, restoring ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Aging at 600°C is expected to induce a ductile-to-brittle transition due to strong ordering and adverse phase boundary characteristics, whereas aging at 750°C should restore ductility and possibly improve overall toughness while maintaining strength.
generation.baseline: Properties of the as-cast alloy without subsequent aging.
generation.boundary: This mechanism and effect magnitude may be specific to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 composition and the aging conditions used; different compositions or processing conditions could yield different phase evolution behaviors.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative changes in mechanical properties and the precise domain size evolution require further empirical validation, and the universality of the response across all Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples and subject them to isothermal aging at 600°C and 750°C for 20 hours under controlled heating and cooling conditions. Following aging, rapidly quench the samples in water to freeze the microstructure. Perform tensile and impact tests to assess mechanical performance and use TEM and APT techniques to characterize the size, ordering, and morphology of the L1₂ domains and phase boundaries.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not show a significant difference in phase ordering (i.e., L1₂ domain characteristics and phase boundary morphology) and corresponding mechanical behavior between the 600°C and 750°C treatments (specifically, if embrittlement is not observed at 600°C or ductility is not restored at 750°C), then the hypothesis that isothermal aging controls phase evolution and mechanical performance in the predicted manner will be falsified.
